newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwait bourse booms in '96, to continue in '97.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait bourse booms in '96, to continue in '97.

text.p: Kuwait's bourse is expected to maintain the upward trend witnessed in 1996 thanks to confidence in the economy, stability and privatisations, officials and dealers said on Saturday.
"God willing; we expect an increase in trade this year," General Secretary of the Union of Arab Stock Exchanges and Securities Commissions Sa'faq al-Rukeibi told Reuters.
"We have stability and there is confidence in the economy," added Rukeibi, also a Kuwait Stock Exchange official.

The share index rose some 40 percent at the end of 1996 to 1905.6 points. Value of traded shares rose 202 percent to 5.760 billion dinars ($19.3 billion) in 1996 compared to 1995 and volume rose 184 percent to 25.7 billion shares in the same period, an Exchange official said.
"If you invest your money across the board (in all listed shares) you could get 10 percent on your money. That is why I expect more active trade in 1997," said a portfolio manager.
The central bank discount rate stands at 7.25 percent. Inflation runs at some 3.0 percent in 1996, according to private estimates.
Economists say the state halving its projected budget deficit, high oil prices and the state's repayement of a jumbo sovereign loan are reasons for increased confidence in the economy.

Higher than expected oil prices have helped Kuwait to slash a projected 1.32 billion dinars deficit in the 1995/96 fiscal year (July-June) to 653 million. They also helped raise GDP at current prices by 8.2 percent to 7.952 billion dinars in 1995.
Kuwait also completed repayment of a $5.5 billion sovereign loan in December without having to sell any foreign assets.
"Privatisation, under a solid economy, would always be a reason for increased activity in the market," said a dealer.

A privatisation plan aims at selling the state's stake in some 60 firms and preparing for a second and more difficult phase to shed state involvement in some public services like water, electricity and telecommunications.
Finance Minister Nasser al-Rodhan has said he hopes to kick off the second phase of the plan during 1997.
A World Bank expert has said the Exchange's chances of being a regional centre would rise if the state removed restrictions on foreign investment and improved further securities regulations.

Only nationals of Gulf Arab states -- Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman and Kuwait -- can trade on the exchange. Kuwait's foreign residents are allowed to take part in mutual funds run by Kuwaiti firms.
Kuwait has said it was considering a plan to remove the ban on foreign participation but no time frame was set.
"This (opening trade for foreigners) is a necessity," said Rukeibi.
